title: Phytochemical-rich fraction from raw and cooked kodo millet ( Paspalum scrobiculatum  L.) reduced the viability of colorectal- and breast cancer cells  in vitro  by inducing apoptosis
content: Kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum L.) is one of the underexplored minor millets with diverse phytochemical composition. Prior studies have shown that phytochemicals such as phenolic acids and tannins of kodo millet can prevent the progression of cancer cells by mitigating oxidative stress and preventing the DNA damage. However, to date, no studies have shown the impact of cooking on the composition and antiproliferative potential of kodo millet free phenolics. Hence, this study is designed to determine the impact of cooking on the phytochemical composition and cytotoxic potential of the hydroalcoholic extract prepared from cooked kodo millet. We found that quercetin, isorhamnetin, apigenin, rutin and ferulic acid are the major compounds found in raw and cooked kodo millet extract when analyzed by LC-HRMS/MS. Interestingly, the cooked kodo millet extract (KMC) (IC50 = 0.14 ± 0.03 mg mL−1) exhibited enhanced cytotoxicity and selectivity towards cancer cells (MDA-MB-231) compared to raw kodo millet extract (KMR) (IC50 = 0.22 ± 0.06 mg mL−1) at 48 hours of treatment. Bioactivity-guided fractionation of these extracts revealed variations in the composition. Quercetin was enriched up to 5-fold in the potent fraction (KM75) derived from KMR extract. However, a 0.6-fold decrease in quercetin content was observed in KMC extract. Interestingly, quercetin was not detected in the insoluble material KMIS. KM75, fraction of KMR exhibited the highest cytotoxic potential (IC50 = 0.11 ± 0.23 mg mL−1) compared to KMIS (IC50 = 0.29 ± 0.08 mg mL−1) fraction of KMC against MDA-MB-231 cell line at 48 hours of treatment. Mechanistically, KM75 has accelerated the progression of cells from early to late apoptotic stages. In summary, the results of our study, for the first time, demonstrated the impact of cooking on kodo millet phytochemical composition and its antiproliferative potential. Further studies (a) investigating the mechanistic basis of identified potent fraction; (b) validating the efficacy in xenografted tumor models in mice and (c) evaluating the potency in patient-derived xenograft model are warranted to establish its efficacy as a chemosensitizer or adjuvant therapy in the treatment of cancer.
